entry.title: Kafka Tutorial: Message Queue with Spring Boot and Kafka

link.title: Kafka Tutorial: Message Queue with Spring Boot and Kafka

entry.content:
Kafka is a distributed streaming platform designed for high throughput, fault tolerance, and scalability. In this tutorial, we will learn how to set up a Kafka message queue using Spring Boot and Kafka for publishing and consuming messages.

What is Kafka?

  • Distributed Streaming Platform: Kafka allows you to stream data across multiple producers and consumers, ensuring fault tolerance and scalability.
  • Publish-Subscribe Messaging Model: Kafka operates using a publish-subscribe model where producers publish messages to topics, and consumers subscribe to those topics.

Kafka’s Key Components:

  • Producers: Applications or microservices that produce data (events) and send them to Kafka topics.
  • Consumers: Applications or microservices that consume data from Kafka topics, processing or storing it as needed.
  • Kafka Brokers: Distributed servers that store data and manage Kafka topics.
  • ZooKeeper: Coordinates the Kafka brokers, maintaining their configuration and leadership.
  • Topics: Kafka topics are where data is stored. Topics are partitioned and replicated for durability.

Setting Up Kafka in a Spring Boot Application

Here’s how you can set up Kafka with Spring Boot and test it by publishing messages via REST APIs.

1. Add Dependencies

Add the following dependencies in your pom.xml file:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.kafka</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-kafka</artifactId>
</dependency>

2. Application Configuration (application.yml)

Make sure you have the correct application properties to point to your Kafka broker:

spring:
  application:
    name: kafka-example
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
  profiles:
    active: dev

3. Set Up Kafka Broker Using Docker Compose

Use Docker Compose to run Kafka locally. Here’s a simple configuration:

services:
  broker:
    image: apache/kafka:latest
    hostname: broker
    container_name: broker
    ports:
      - 9092:9092
    environment:
      KAFKA_BROKER_ID: 1
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://broker:29092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_LOG_DIRS: /tmp/kraft-combined-logs
      CLUSTER_ID: MkU3OEVBNTcwNTJENDM2Qk

Configure Kafka Topics

To create Kafka topics programmatically, add this configuration:

package com.kafka.kafka_example.config;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.kafka.config.TopicBuilder;
@Configuration
public class KafkaTopicConfig {
    @Bean
    public NewTopic topic() {
        return TopicBuilder.name("my-first-topic").build();
    }
}

Configure Kafka Producer

Configure the Kafka producer to send messages to Kafka topics:

package com.kafka.kafka_example.config;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerConfig;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.DefaultKafkaProducerFactory;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.ProducerFactory;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
@Configuration
public class KafkaProducerConfig {
    @Value("${spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers}")
    private String bootstrapServers;
    public Map<String, Object> KafkaProducerConfig() {
        HashMap<String, Object> props = new HashMap<>();
        props.put(ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, bootstrapServers);
        props.put(ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class);
        props.put(ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class);
        return props;
    }
    @Bean // Dependency Injection
    public ProducerFactory<String, String> KafkaProducerFactory() {
        return new DefaultKafkaProducerFactory<>(KafkaProducerConfig());
    }
    @Bean
    public KafkaTemplate<String, String> KafkaTemplate(ProducerFactory<String, String> ProducerFactory) {
        return new KafkaTemplate<>(ProducerFactory);
    }
}

Configure Kafka Consumer

Configure the Kafka consumer to listen to messages from the topic:

package com.kafka.kafka_example.config;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerConfig;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.kafka.config.ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.ConsumerFactory;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.DefaultKafkaConsumerFactory;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
@Configuration
public class KafkaConsumerConfig {
    @Value("${spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers}")
    private String bootstrapServers;
    @Bean
    public Map<String, Object> consumerConfigProperties() {
        HashMap<String, Object> props = new HashMap<>();
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, bootstrapServers);
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class);
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class);
        return props;
    }
    @Bean
    public ConsumerFactory<String, String> kafkaConsumerFactory() {
        return new DefaultKafkaConsumerFactory<>(consumerConfigProperties());
    }
    @Bean
    public ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, String> kafkaListenerContainerFactory(ConsumerFactory<String, String> kafkaConsumerFactory) {
        ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, String> factory = new ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<>();
        factory.setConsumerFactory(kafkaConsumerFactory);
        return factory;
    }
}

Test Kafka Producer and Consumer with Command Line

Run this command to check if Kafka is running correctly:

bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-first-topic --from-beginning

Create Kafka Listener

To receive messages from Kafka, create a Kafka listener class:

package com.kafka.kafka_example;
import org.springframework.kafka.annotation.KafkaListener;
public class KafkaListeners {
    @KafkaListener(
            topics = "my-first-topic",  // Topic to listen to
            groupId = "group-id"        // Consumer group ID
    )
    void listener(String data) {
        System.out.println("Listener received: " + data);  // Print message to console
    }
}

Create a RESTful API to Publish Messages

Now, let’s create a simple REST API to publish messages to Kafka:

package com.kafka.kafka_example.Controller;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
@RestController
public class MessageController {
    private KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafkaTemplate;
    public MessageController(KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }
    @PostMapping("/api/v1/messages")
    public void publishMessage(@RequestBody String message) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("my-first-topic", message);
    }
}

Test the REST API

You can now test the REST API by sending a POST request to /api/v1/messages with a message payload, and the message will be published to the Kafka topic.

Conclusion

In this tutorial, you learned how to set up Kafka in a Spring Boot application, configure Kafka producers and consumers, and test Kafka messaging with a RESTful API. You also saw how to set up Kafka using Docker Compose for local development.

Check Kafka Broker Status

You can use this command to check if your Kafka broker is running:

bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic my-first-topic --from-beginning

entry.title: How I Passed the OCI AI Foundations Associate

link.title: How I Passed the OCI AI Foundations Associate

entry.content:
Achieving the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) AI Foundations Associate (2023) certification was a significant milestone in my career. This certification validated my knowledge and skills in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) within the OCI ecosystem. Here’s a detailed breakdown of how I navigated through the course and prepared for the certification exam.

Course Overview

The OCI AI Foundations course is meticulously structured to provide a comprehensive understanding of AI and ML fundamentals, OCI AI services, and best practices. The course is divided into four main parts:

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure AI Foundations Course

Prepare for OCI AI Foundations Associate Certification

Practice Exam: OCI AI Foundations Certification

Final Exam: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure 2023 AI Foundations Associate (1Z0–1122–23)

Part 1: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure AI Foundations Course

Course Content

The first part of the course lays the groundwork for understanding AI and ML concepts. It covers:

- AI Terminology : Essential terms such as machine learning, deep learning, data science, and neural networks.
- OCI AI Services and Infrastructure: An exploration of the AI services and infrastructure offered by Oracle.
- Generative AI Basics: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and Transformers.
- AI and ML Best Practices: Guidelines for designing, developing, and deploying robust AI solutions.

Each section of this part ends with a skills check, comprising five questions to test your understanding of the material. These quizzes are crucial as they mirror the type of questions you will encounter in the final exam.

Part 2: Prepare for OCI AI Foundations Associate Certification

Preparation Module

This module is designed to refresh and consolidate your knowledge in preparation for the certification exam. It includes:

- Review of Exam Objectives: A detailed look at the topics covered in the exam.
- Understanding Key Topics: Refreshing your grasp on crucial concepts.
- Resource Identification: Listing available materials for further study.
- Sample Questions: Practicing with a few example questions to familiarize yourself with the exam format.

The 17-minute video in this section provides valuable insights into the exam structure and the types of questions previously posed.

Part 3: Practice Exam: OCI AI Foundations Certification

Importance of Practice

The practice exam is an essential part of the preparation process. It allows you to:

- Test Your Knowledge: Identify areas where you need more study.
- Familiarize with Exam Format: Get used to the style and format of the actual exam questions.
- Identify Repeated Questions: Many questions from the practice exam appear in the final exam, making this an invaluable resource.

Part 4: Final Exam: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure 2023 AI Foundations Associate (1Z0–1122–23)

Exam Strategy

Having thoroughly prepared through the first three parts of the course, I felt confident when taking the final exam. Key strategies included:

- Regular Review: Continuously revisiting course materials and notes.
- Skill Checks: Regularly taking the skills check quizzes to ensure retention of information.
- Practice Exam: Taking the practice exam multiple times to ensure familiarity with the question format and content.

Conclusion

Passing the OCI AI Foundations Associate certification exam required a structured and disciplined approach. The course content was comprehensive, and the preparation modules were crucial in reinforcing my knowledge. By leveraging the provided resources and consistently testing my understanding, I was able to successfully pass the exam and achieve my certification. This accomplishment has not only enhanced my credentials but also deepened my expertise in AI and ML within the OCI environment.
